meta.description: Versioned, comparable pipelines and neural-data governance for neurotechnology teams. Pre-release: not deployed, no customers yet.

hero.heading: Evidence layer for regulated neural data.
hero.lede: Neurotech teams need to show what was done to their data and what they are allowed to do with it. Several state neural-data laws are in force, and none of the neural-data tools and services in our market review offers neural-specific consent, deletion and audit.

banner: Pre-release. Not deployed. No customers yet.

sections.heading: Why this matters now.
body: Results depend on preprocessing choices that are rarely shared, and the laws that now cover neural data do not agree on what it is.

items.heading: Preprocessing choices change results
items.body: Artifact correction and filter settings change decoding performance, and in one comparison of dozens of pipelines, none was best overall.

items.heading: Few papers share their pipelines
items.body: A systematic review of EEG-BCI publications found that only a minority made their code or pipelines available.

items.heading: States disagree on what neural data is
items.body: Colorado and California cover the central or peripheral nervous system; Connecticut covers the central nervous system only. One EMG or EEG recording can be neural data in one state and not in the next.

items.heading: Clinical teams need documented evidence
items.body: FDA guidance says implanted BCIs should generally follow the Enhanced Documentation Level for device software.

evidence.text: All artifact-correction steps reduced decoding performance; higher high-pass cutoffs increased it (Kessler et al., Commun Biol 2025).
Across 43 pipelines there was "no single best pipeline" (Huang et al., Psychophysiology 2025).
Of 129 EEG-BCI publications, 20.9% made code or pipelines available (Peksa et al., Sensors 2026).

Colorado HB24-1058 and California SB 1223 define neural data by the central or peripheral nervous system; Connecticut PA 25-113 by the central nervous system only; California excludes data inferred from non-neural information.

Our review of 22 neural-data tools and services (e.g. BrainFlow, LSL, MNE-Python, DANDI, OpenNeuro, Flywheel, AWS) found no neural-specific privacy tooling; every open tool lacks consent, deletion and audit features.
FDA's implanted BCI guidance (issued 20 May 2021) notes that implanted BCIs "should generally address the recommendations for an Enhanced Documentation Level".

sections.heading: The regulatory driver.
body: Neural data has moved into protected categories in several US states, the EU restricts emotion inference, and investors are funding neurotech devices.

items.heading: State laws in force
items.body: Colorado, California and Connecticut have enacted neural-data protections, and a peer-reviewed review reports that Montana has too. A federal bill, the MIND Act, has been introduced.

items.heading: EU limits on emotion models
items.body: The EU AI Act bans emotion inference in workplace and education settings, except for medical or safety reasons.

items.heading: Implants moving into clinical use
items.body: Implant makers have received FDA clearances and clinical-study approvals.

items.heading: Capital is reaching the sector
items.body: In the year covered by the cited review, neurotech devices drew more venture funding than any other type of medical device.

evidence.text: Colorado HB24-1058 effective 7 Aug 2024; California SB 1223 chaptered 28 Sep 2024; Connecticut PA 25-113 signed 24 Jun 2025, CTDPA sections effective 1 Jul 2026.
Montana adopted SB 163 in May 2025, per Cabrera et al., Bioethics 2026. The statute text itself has not been opened.
The MIND Act was introduced in September 2025 and directs an FTC study (Young, Simon & Evans, Neurology 2026). Bill number and current status not verified.
EU AI Act Art. 5(1)(f) bans AI that infers emotions in workplace and education, except for medical or safety reasons; applicable from 2 Feb 2025.
Precision Neuroscience: FDA 510(k) clearance Apr 2025. Paradromics: IDE approved Nov 2025.
In 2024, "neurotechnology companies received $1.2 billion in venture capital funding, more than any other type of medical device" (Ruiz-Mateos Serrano et al., Sci Adv 2026, citing HSBC).

sections.heading: What we are building.
body: One lineage graph over neural data, pipelines and models, with products built on it. Core modules are built and tested internally; none is deployed, published or in use by a customer.

items.heading: Open Core SDK
items.body: A Python SDK with local provenance, designed to work alongside MNE, BIDS, NWB and LSL rather than replace them. Planned as open source; not yet published.

items.heading: Multiverse audit
items.body: Runs a grid of preprocessing pipelines and reports how results shift, with every parameter recorded. The sweep engine is built; the study on public data has not been run.

items.heading: Consent & Deletion Ledger
items.body: Per-channel jurisdiction classification, versioned consent, and withdrawal that reaches raw data, derivatives and trained models, with a signed deletion certificate.

items.heading: FDA Evidence Kit
items.body: Traceability, SBOM and off-the-shelf software documentation scaffolds generated from the lineage graph. A scaffold, not a regulatory submission.

items.heading: Governed model registry
items.body: Model provenance with use-restriction flags, so an emotion model cannot be deployed where the EU AI Act prohibits it.

sections.heading: Controls built in.
body: Governance controls that are built and tested internally. They have not been audited externally.

items.heading: Crypto-shredding
items.body: Per-subject encryption keys, so deleting a key makes that subject's data unreadable, including the backup copy, while other subjects stay readable.

items.heading: Tamper-evident lineage
items.body: Changing a node, edge or batch in the provenance graph fails verification.

items.heading: Consent check on every data route
items.body: Every route that touches data calls one consent-policy check, and training without the training consent scope is denied.

sections.heading: What could compound.
body: Three advantages we plan to build. None is established yet.

items.heading: Machine-readable neural-law rules
items.body: Versioned rules per jurisdiction, which already generate the public law tracker. Counsel review is still pending, so the rules are marked unverified where they have not been checked.

items.heading: The lineage graph as system of record
items.body: Once consent, pipeline runs and model versions live in one graph, deletion certificates and FDA evidence come from it, which creates switching cost.

items.heading: Published reproducibility evidence
items.body: Multiverse results on public datasets could become citable references. No results have been published yet.

sections.heading: Planned go-to-market sequence.
body: First: release the open-core SDK and publish the multiverse study on public data. Next: the ledger and a startup tier, recruiting design partners. Then: the FDA Evidence Kit and a first pharma pilot. This is a plan; no step has started with customers.

sections.heading: What you can open today.
body: The Neural Playground is an offline demo on open monkey motor-cortex data. It is not the platform's evaluation engine.
The Decoder Arena is in development. The law tracker is generated at build time from the rule files in the repository.
